Triggers.value: A specific texture associated with the event
A specific temperature on the skin

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
I distract myself with something else

Threat.value: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I have lost my connection to my community and culture

vignette:
Kofi presents as a quiet, watchful 27-year-old man, his body held in a state of coiled stillness that seems at odds with the constant motion of his life as an Uber driver. The trauma he describes is not a single event, but a period of years in his early adolescence after arriving in the U.S. to live with an uncle. The memories are fragmented, often returning not as a clear narrative but as powerful sensory intrusions. He speaks of a basement, of the hollow sound of his uncle’s heavy footsteps on the wooden stairs overhead, a sound that always preceded a beating. He remembers the specific cold of the concrete floor against his cheek and, most vividly, the coarse, scratchy texture of the burlap sacks he was sometimes forced to kneel on. These sensations have become anchors for his fear, tethering his present to the past without his consent.

His life is now a carefully curated attempt to manage these sensory ambushes. Driving offers a semblance of control, yet his car is also a primary arena for his struggles. He is hypervigilant to a degree that exhausts him, his eyes constantly scanning mirrors and sidewalks, his mind assessing every passenger for potential threat. The sound of someone walking up behind his car at a red light can cause his heart to hammer against his ribs, his hands to slick with sweat on the steering wheel. He has come to see his own body as an enemy, a traitor that erupts into panic for reasons he knows are illogical. "I am safe, I'm in a locked car," he explains, "but my body doesn't believe it. It thinks the footsteps are on the stairs again." A passenger once tossed a canvas duffel bag onto the seat beside him, and the rough texture under his hand sent a jolt of ice through his veins, forcing him to pull over until the wave of nausea passed. He turns the radio up loud, losing himself in talk shows and music for hours on end, a constant wall of sound to keep the memories at bay.

Over the years, these protective measures have calcified into a profound isolation. Kofi is single and has not been in a serious relationship. He finds himself unable to tolerate emotional closeness, deflecting personal questions from well-meaning passengers and keeping acquaintances at a safe, superficial distance. The idea of being vulnerable with someone feels impossibly dangerous. This isolation extends to his community. On weekends, he sees other Ghanaian men from his neighborhood gathering at parks or restaurants, their laughter carrying on the breeze, and he feels a deep, aching sense of loss. He is certain they would not understand, that the damage inside him has made him fundamentally different, severing his connection to the culture that should be his home. He holds the conviction that he has been permanently changed for the worse, that the boy he was before the basement is gone forever.

His nights are spent in a small apartment where he never truly feels safe. He checks the locks repeatedly, but the feeling of security remains elusive. Most evenings, he smokes marijuana until the sharp edges of his anxiety are dulled into a manageable haze. Paradoxically, this constant internal threat has also led him to take external risks. He will sometimes accept late-night fares to notoriously dangerous neighborhoods or drive far too fast on empty highways, chasing a thrill that momentarily eclipses his fear with a feeling of agency. It was after one such night, following a near-miss on the interstate, that the full weight of his exhaustion hit him. He realized his strategies were not keeping him safe but were instead shrinking his world and putting him in real danger. He came to therapy not with a clear hope, but with a desperate question: whether it was possible to ever feel safe inside his own skin again, to convince his body that the footsteps are no longer coming.
